entries.clue: Short shabby detective – US – I went there! (8)

indicatorNotes.Short: a short word is cut down: COLUMBO loses its last letter

blocks.note: Columbo, the scruffy TV detective in the raincoat, cut short
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A breathless tourist's postcard boasting about visiting the home of a scruffy American TV detective.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken by the answer: Columbus could say of the US 'I went there!' The exclamation mark flags the playful definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Christopher Columbus sailed to the Americas, so he might say of the US that he went there.

entries.clue: Feuding family’s pills laced with uranium (8)

indicatorNotes.laced with: the pills are laced with, so contain, the extra ingredient

blocks.note: caplets are capsule-shaped tablets
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

annotation.surface: A poisoning plot: a family's medicine spiked with something radioactive.
annotation.walkthrough: The poisoned pills fit the Romeo and Juliet story, where potions and poison decide everything.
annotation.definitionFit: The Capulets are Juliet's family, locked in a feud with the Montagues.

entries.clue: ‘Animal star sign.’ ‘Chameleon?’ ‘Not entirely.’ (3)

indicatorNotes.Not entirely: only part of the word is used, so the answer sits inside it

blocks.note: the three letters sit in the middle of the lizard's name, after CHAME

annotation.surface: A snatch of dialogue: someone asks which star sign is an animal, another suggests chameleon, and is told 'not quite'.
annotation.walkthrough: The quiz-show exchange is the disguise: 'Not entirely' reads as a verdict on the guess, but it tells you to take part of CHAMELEON.
annotation.definitionFit: Leo, the lion, is a sign of the zodiac named after an animal.

entries.clue: Brief moments with that French woman – and wine (7)

blocks.note: mo is short for moment, as in 'half a mo'
elle is French for 'she'

annotation.surface: A romantic snatched interlude with a Frenchwoman over a glass of wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'with' simply joins the two pieces in order.
annotation.definitionFit: Moselle is a white wine from the Moselle valley in Germany and Luxembourg.

entries.clue: ‘Undecorated’? Right to get rise, as base layer’s been applied (11)

indicatorNotes.Right to get rise: the R (right) moves up the word, which in a down entry means earlier

blocks.note: the word as printed, in quotation marks
move R from after UNDECO to after UNDE

annotation.surface: A decorator's note: a bare surface isn't really undecorated once the undercoat is on.
annotation.walkthrough: Not a free shuffle: only the R moves. In UNDECORATED it sits after UNDECO; lift it two places and you get UNDE-R-COATED.
annotation.definitionFit: Something undercoated has had its base layer of paint put on.

entries.clue: English: scratching head, unable to qualify (6)

indicatorNotes.scratching head: scratching out the head removes the first letter

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
UNABLE without its first letter

annotation.surface: A pupil scratching their head over an English exam they can't pass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'scratching head' reads as puzzlement but means delete the first letter; E then takes the vanished U's place.
annotation.definitionFit: To enable someone is to qualify them, make them fit or able to do something.

entries.clue: Amateur artist to capture rising waterfall (7)

indicatorNotes.rising: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom up

blocks.note: A = amateur
RA = Royal Academician
to gain is to capture or win

annotation.surface: A Sunday painter setting out to get a rushing waterfall onto canvas.
annotation.walkthrough: A, RA and GAIN make ARAGAIN, which reads upwards as NIAGARA.
annotation.definitionFit: Niagara Falls is the famous waterfall on the US–Canada border.

entries.clue: Great amounts rain heavily on blokes protecting duck (11)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down entry, one piece sits on top of the next

blocks.note: it's bucketing down
lads = blokes
a duck in cricket is a score of nought, O

annotation.surface: Men sheltering a duck from a downpour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'duck' pretends to be the bird sheltering from the rain; in cricket it is a score of nothing, hence O.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal British measure: a bucketload is as much as a bucket holds, so bucketloads means plenty.

entries.clue: In placid manner, pick six characters from seven lycanthropes (6)

indicatorNotes.pick six characters from: take six letters running straight through the words that follow

blocks.note: start after the S of seven and run across the word break for six letters

annotation.surface: Calmly choosing six out of a line-up of seven werewolves.
annotation.walkthrough: The six characters sound like werewolves to pick, but they are letters. A lycanthrope is a werewolf.
annotation.definitionFit: To speak evenly is to speak calmly, in a placid manner.

entries.clue: Edward by island on sailboat, reversing at water’s edge (8)

indicatorNotes.reversing: the whole string is read backwards
indicatorNotes.by: 'by' in the sense of 'beside', so Edward stands next to the island
indicatorNotes.on: the island comes before the sailboat

blocks.note: Ed is short for Edward
I = island
a sloop is a single-masted sailing boat

annotation.surface: Edward sailing a small boat past an island, turning back near the shore.
annotation.walkthrough: ED, I and SLOOP make EDISLOOP, which reads backwards as POOLSIDE.
annotation.definitionFit: Poolside means beside a pool, at the water's edge.

entries.clue: Awkward, grand and long – at the outset, uncle’s hosted (6)

indicatorNotes.at the outset: take the first letter of uncle
indicatorNotes.hosted: the ache holds the U as its guest

blocks.note: G = grand, a thousand pounds
to long for is to ache for
first letter of uncle

annotation.surface: An uncle playing host to someone clumsy, grand and tall.
annotation.walkthrough: U goes into ACHE to make AUCHE, with G in front. 'long' looks like an adjective but is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Gauche means socially awkward or clumsy.

entries.clue: Everyman is improperly described by two lines making damaging accusation (5)

indicatorNotes.described by: to describe is also to draw round, so the lines enclose the middle

blocks.note: L = line, twice
the setter is I, and 'I be' is ungrammatical for 'I am'

annotation.surface: A complaint that the setter has been misrepresented in a couple of lines of print.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman is the setter, so 'Everyman is' becomes I + BE, the improper form of 'I am'. 'described' means drawn around: L-IBE-L.
annotation.definitionFit: A libel is a published false statement that damages someone's reputation.

entries.clue: Ones drawing fictional pig? They appeal to the girls (4-7)

blocks.note: Babe is the sheep-herding pig of the novel and film
magnets draw things towards them

annotation.surface: Something that attracts a famous fictional pig turns out to be irresistible to women.
annotation.walkthrough: Read cryptically, magnets for Babe are things that draw the pig. The question mark marks the whimsy.
annotation.definitionFit: Babe magnets is slang for men, or things like flash cars, that attract women.

entries.clue: Squeeze a beauty, we’re told, to arouse memories (4,1,4)

indicatorNotes.we’re told: what we hear rather than what is written

blocks.note: wring = squeeze; a belle is a beauty

annotation.surface: Hugging an old flame to jog the memory.
annotation.walkthrough: WRING and RING, BELLE and BELL sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: When something rings a bell, it stirs a faint memory.

entries.clue: What the absent-minded (or uncaring) greengrocer does (3,4,1,3)

annotation.definition: What the absent-minded (or uncaring) greengrocer does

blocks.note: the literal reading: a forgetful shopkeeper fails to hand over one piece of fruit
the idiomatic reading: someone who could not care less

annotation.surface: A fruit seller who forgets part of your order.
annotation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(or uncaring)' points to the idiom, while the greengrocer makes it literal.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a fig stands for something worthless, so to withhold even that is to be utterly indifferent.

entries.clue: Postpone unit’s dance and indoor game (5,8)

blocks.note: in US usage, to table a motion is to postpone it
a foot is a unit of length
a ball is a formal dance

annotation.surface: A military unit putting off its dance and playing a game indoors instead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'unit' suggests soldiers, but it is the measurement. Table football is the game with rods of little players, also called foosball.
annotation.definitionFit: Table football is a tabletop game played indoors.

entries.clue: Doesn’t leave out trendy crosswords’ building blocks: about 500! (8)

blocks.note: in = fashionable
a crossword is built from clues
D is 500 in Roman numerals

annotation.surface: A fashionable crossword-lover insisting on about 500 clues.
annotation.walkthrough: 'about 500' reads as an estimate of how many clues, but it places the Roman numeral inside them.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by negation: the opposite of excluding, so 'doesn't leave out' is a plain synonym phrase.

entries.clue: Range of human inaction unsettling (8,5)

indicatorNotes.unsettling: the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A complaint that people's idleness is disturbing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Range' reads as scope, as in the range of human behaviour, but it is a line of mountains.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the geographical sense: a range is a connected line of peaks.

entries.clue: Upriver, glimpsed along Nile’s drainage area: national, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Upriver, glimpsed along Nile’s drainage area: national, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: in the first place, so each word gives its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: Upriver, glimpsed along Nile’s drainage area: national
blocks.note: seven words, each contributing its first letter

annotation.surface: A traveller spotting someone upstream in the Nile basin and guessing their nationality.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: Uganda lies upriver in the Nile's drainage basin, and its national is a Ugandan.
annotation.definitionFit: Uganda contains the Nile's upper reaches, so a national glimpsed there would be Ugandan.

entries.clue: Relate to sorrow (7)

blocks.note: a verb: to be about or have a bearing on something
a noun: worry or distress on someone's behalf

annotation.walkthrough: 'Relate to' suggests empathising with someone's sorrow, but it means 'be about'.
annotation.definitionFit: Concern means both to be about something and a feeling of worry or distress.

entries.clue: Literary figure found meandering in Detroit, mostly (6)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word but not all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: DETROIT without its last T

annotation.surface: A literary celebrity spotted wandering around Detroit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Literary figure' suggests an author or a character, but an editor works in literature too.
annotation.definitionFit: An editor is a figure in the literary world, preparing others' writing for print.

entries.clue: On track, bat’s simple stroke (3,6)

indicatorNotes.On: the track comes first, placed on the bat

blocks.note: to dog someone is to track them
a table-tennis bat is also called a paddle

annotation.surface: A cricketer on track, praising a batsman's easy shot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'bat' and 'stroke' suggest cricket, but the stroke is a swimming one.
annotation.definitionFit: The dog paddle is the simplest swimming stroke, paddling like a dog.

entries.clue: Nosy astronauts left (5)

blocks.note: NASA is the US space agency, employer of astronauts
L = left

annotation.surface: Inquisitive astronauts have left.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nosy' looks like prying but means 'of the nose'.
annotation.definitionFit: Nasal means relating to the nose, which is nosy in a literal sense.

entries.clue: Studious, tense and wimpish (6)

blocks.note: T = tense, in grammar
weedy = feeble, wimpish

annotation.surface: A portrait of a nervous, bookish weakling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'tense' reads as anxious, fitting the wimp, but it is the grammatical abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Tweedy describes the bookish, academic type in tweed jackets.

entries.clue: Swayed, being camp (8)

blocks.note: influenced
exaggerated, mannered

annotation.surface: Someone moving their hips theatrically.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swayed' tempts as physical movement, but it means influenced.
annotation.definitionFit: Affected means both influenced and artificially showy.

entries.clue: Stoves regularly seen in sets (3)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: s-T-o-V-e-S

annotation.surface: Cookers routinely found in matched sets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'sets' suggests matching kitchen equipment, but it means television sets.
annotation.definitionFit: A shortening: 'set' alone has long meant a television or radio receiver, as in 'switch on the set'.

entries.clue: Once again despatched gift without slightest hint of provocation (6)

indicatorNotes.without: the gift goes without, that is lacks, the letter that follows
indicatorNotes.slightest hint of: only the first letter of provocation

blocks.note: a present is a gift
first letter of provocation, removed

annotation.surface: Returning a present that was sent unprovoked.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is read as RE-SENT, not the verb 'resent', which the word 'provocation' hints at.
annotation.definitionFit: Re-sent means dispatched once again.

entries.clue: Suffers sea song I butchered (8)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A singer apologising for mangling a sea shanty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suffers' could be the listeners' reaction to the butchered song.
annotation.definitionFit: To agonise is to suffer anguish.
